article.headline: Uranium and Digital Biology: The AI Boom's Overlooked Beneficiaries
article.lede: An influential crypto-finance account argues that investors crowded into semiconductor and memory stocks are missing two quieter beneficiaries of the AI era: uranium, where a structural supply deficit meets surging data-center power demand, and digital biology, where artificial intelligence is rewiring pharmaceutical discovery. The post appears to be the closing line of a longer thread, but its core claim stands without further context.
article.body:
The tweet begins mid-thought — almost certainly the tail of a longer thread — but the argument is familiar in commodity and biotech circles: the obvious trade has been discovered, priced, and crowded, while the less-obvious one has not. The poster's “YW” (you’re welcome) is crypto-Twitter shorthand for a high-conviction tip delivered with pointed nonchalance.

Since 2023, institutional capital has flooded into semiconductors and memory. Nvidia (NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), SK Hynix (000660.KS), and Micron Technology (MU) all rode the same thesis: build AI infrastructure, buy more chips. SK Hynix’s operating margin reached 58 percent on surging demand for *HBM* (high-bandwidth memory) from Nvidia. By April 2026, BTIG’s chief market technician noted that the spread between software stocks and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had reached extremes not seen since the dot-com era — a warning that when a trade becomes consensus, expected forward returns compress.

Uranium’s investment case is structural rather than cyclical. Global production has chronically lagged consumption: the industry contracted 589 million pounds over the five years through 2025 while consuming 815 million. Cameco (CCJ), the largest Western producer, estimates cumulative uncovered utility requirements through 2045 at roughly 3.1 billion pounds. Kazatomprom (KAP), which commands about 45 percent of global output, cut its 2026 production guidance from 85 million to 77 million pounds — signaling no incentive to flood the market. Long-term contract prices hit a 14-year high of $86.50 per pound in December 2025, still just below the threshold at which new mine development becomes economically justifiable, meaning the deficit has years to run before supply responds meaningfully. The AI connection is direct: data-center electricity consumption surged 17 percent in 2025, per the International Energy Agency, and tech companies are signing nuclear power-purchase agreements at pace, with conditional *SMR* (small modular reactor) offtake commitments growing from 25 gigawatts at end-2024 to 45 gigawatts by early 2026. Developers like NexGen Energy (NXE) — whose Arrow deposit in Saskatchewan grades at 3.10 percent *U3O8* (triuranium octoxide, the standard commercial form of uranium), roughly 25 to 40 times richer than the global average, and which received its construction licence in March 2026 — and Uranium Energy Corp (UEC), which opened the first new *ISR* (in-situ recovery) uranium mine in the United States in over a decade in April 2026, represent the higher-risk end of a supply response still years from closing the structural gap.

**Digital biology** — the poster’s second theme — is shorthand for applying AI to biological discovery. The field’s most legible proof of concept arrived with DeepMind’s AlphaFold 3 (May 2024), which extended protein-structure prediction to multi-molecule interactions, enabling computational drug design at scale. If software can predict how proteins, DNA, RNA, and small molecules interact, the pharmaceutical industry’s historically expensive discovery pipeline compresses dramatically. Recursion Pharmaceuticals (RXRX), backed by Nvidia, screens over 15 billion compounds via AI and acquired Exscientia in November 2024, adding more than 20 clinical programs. Ginkgo Bioworks (DNA) designs millions of proteins and biological strains daily, though its revenue fell in early 2026 amid restructuring — a reminder that long development timelines are punishing to companies that need near-term cash. Capital-allocation signals are clearest at the big-pharma end: Earendel Labs raised $787 million in March 2026 from Sanofi (SAN.PA) and Pfizer (PFE) for AI-designed *bispecific antibodies* (engineered proteins that bind two distinct molecular targets simultaneously, widely used in oncology and autoimmune disease), and Eli Lilly (LLY) is building what it calls the most powerful AI supercomputer operated by a pharmaceutical company, in partnership with Nvidia. ARK Invest frames the broader theme as *multiomics* — the convergence of genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics data streams with AI — and treats it as the healthcare trade of the decade.

What unites uranium and digital biology as a paired call is a structural property: both benefit from the same macro forces driving the semiconductor consensus — AI compute buildout, power-hungry infrastructure, AI-driven discovery — without attracting the institutional crowding that has already priced those forces into chip valuations. Uranium is held mainly by specialist commodity investors and physical trusts; digital biology remains thinly followed after the collapse of the ARK Genomic Revolution ETF from its 2021 highs. The caller’s argument, compressed to a sentence, is that the obvious beneficiaries of the AI era have been discovered, owned, and repriced — and the quiet ones have not.

concepts.definition: A type of computer memory designed for extremely high-speed data transfer, achieved by stacking multiple memory chips vertically and connecting them to a processor via a silicon interposer. HBM is essential for training and running large AI models and is the defining feature of Nvidia’s AI accelerators; SK Hynix supplies the majority of global HBM production to Nvidia.

A nuclear fission reactor with an electrical output typically below 300 megawatts, designed to be factory-built and deployed modularly rather than constructed on-site like traditional large nuclear plants. Tech companies including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are signing conditional offtake agreements with SMR developers to secure carbon-free baseload power for AI data centers.

The chemical compound — commonly called yellowcake — in which uranium is commercially traded after ore is mined and processed. Uranium deposit quality is typically quoted as a percentage of U3O8 in rock; the global average for operating mines is well below 0.5 percent, making Arrow’s 3.10 percent grade exceptional.

A uranium mining technique in which a chemical solution is pumped underground to dissolve uranium in place, then pumped back to the surface for extraction. It avoids traditional open-pit or underground mining, produces lower environmental disturbance, and carries lower operating costs; it is the dominant production method in the United States and Kazakhstan.

The integrated analysis of multiple biological data types — genomics (DNA sequences), proteomics (proteins), metabolomics (small-molecule metabolites), and others — using AI models to find patterns across previously siloed datasets. The thesis is that combining these data streams accelerates drug discovery and biomarker identification in ways that any single data type cannot.

Engineered proteins designed to bind two different molecular targets simultaneously — for example, connecting an immune cell to a tumor cell to direct an immune attack. They are widely used in oncology and autoimmune disease; AI is accelerating their design by predicting protein-protein interactions computationally before expensive laboratory synthesis.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_ccj.name: Cameco Corporation
ticker_ccj.blurb: Cameco Corporation is a leading global provider of uranium fuel for nuclear power generation, operating through three segments: Uranium, Fuel Services, and Westinghouse. The Uranium segment explores, mines, and sells uranium concentrate; Fuel Services handles refining, conversion, and fabrication; and Westinghouse is a nuclear reactor technology OEM. Headquartered in Canada, Cameco is one of the world's largest uranium producers and plays a critical role in the nuclear energy supply chain.
ticker_ccj.recent: In the past 30 days, Cameco reported strong earnings on May 5, 2026, with net income surging 161.6% year-over-year to $466.07 million. The stock has traded in a 52-week range of $48.81 to $135.24, closing at $116.75 on May 8, 2026. Analysts maintain a Strong Buy rating with a price target of $123.92, reflecting optimism around nuclear energy demand.

ticker_kap.exchange: London Stock Exchange (XLON) — GDRs; also Astana International Exchange (AIX)
ticker_kap.blurb: National Atomic Company Kazatomprom JSC is the world's largest uranium producer, headquartered in Astana, Kazakhstan. The company accounts for roughly 40% of global primary uranium output, selling uranium concentrates and conversion products to nuclear power operators across Asia, Europe, and North America. Majority-owned by Kazakhstan's sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna, Kazatomprom extracts uranium almost exclusively via low-cost in-situ recovery (ISR) across Kazakhstan's southern uranium deposits. Its global depositary receipts (GDRs) trade on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker KAP.

ticker_rxrx.name: Recursion Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
ticker_rxrx.blurb: Recursion Pharmaceuticals is a clinical-stage TechBio company headquartered in Salt Lake City, Utah, that combines large-scale biological experimentation with machine learning to accelerate drug discovery. The company runs millions of automated cellular experiments weekly, generating proprietary datasets it calls the Recursion OS, which it uses to identify disease mechanisms and novel drug candidates across rare diseases, oncology, and infectious disease. Recursion has strategic partnerships with NVIDIA (which invested $50M in 2023) and Bayer, and completed its acquisition of AI drug-discovery firm Exscientia in 2024, significantly expanding its computational chemistry capabilities. As of mid-2025 it had multiple programs in clinical trials but remained pre-revenue in the traditional pharmaceutical sense.

ticker_pfe.blurb: Pfizer Inc. is a global biopharmaceutical company headquartered in New York City that discovers, develops, manufactures, and commercializes medicines and vaccines across therapeutic areas including oncology, immunology, cardiology, and infectious disease. The company is one of the largest pharmaceutical firms in the world by revenue, with a broad portfolio spanning branded biologics, small molecules, and consumer health products. Pfizer gained significant scale and public attention through its mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine (Comirnaty) and antiviral treatment (Paxlovid), developed in partnership with BioNTech, though revenue from those products has declined sharply from pandemic-era peaks. The company continues to invest heavily in R&D and has pursued large acquisitions—most notably the $43 billion purchase of Seagen in 2023—to build out its oncology pipeline.

Its next-generation triple agonist retatrutide — targeting GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors simultaneously — produced up to 28.7 percent average body weight loss in Phase 3 TRIUMPH trials and is on track for an NDA filing in late 2026 or early 2027, with potential approval in 2027-2028. Lilly also markets Verzenio (breast cancer), Jardiance (diabetes/heart failure), and Taltz (inflammatory disease).
